claim: Learning requires neural adaptations thought to be mediated by activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: Learning requires neural adaptations thought to be mediated by activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between learning and synaptic plasticity, supported by established scientific consensus in neuroscience.

claim: A relatively non-standard form of synaptic plasticity driven by dendritic calcium spikes, or plateau potentials, has been reported to underlie place field formation in rodent hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: A relatively non-standard form of synaptic plasticity driven by dendritic calcium spikes, or plateau potentials, has been reported to underlie place field formation in rodent hippocampal CA1 neurons.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about BTSP and place field formation, implicitly citing previous work.

claim: Behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) can reshape existing place fields via bidirectional synaptic weight changes that depend on the temporal proximity of plateau potentials to pre-existing place fields.
source: Here, we found that this behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) can also reshape existing place fields via bidirectional synaptic weight changes that depend on the temporal proximity of plateau potentials to pre-existing place fields.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When evoked near an existing place field, plateau potentials induced less synaptic potentiation and more depression.
source: When evoked near an existing place field, plateau potentials induced less synaptic potentiation and more depression, suggesting BTSP might depend inversely on postsynaptic activation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: The anti-correlation between plateau potentials and synaptic changes results from a dependence on current synaptic weight such that weak inputs potentiate and strong inputs depress.
source: However, manipulations of place cell membrane potential and computational modeling indicated that this anti-correlation actually results from a dependence on current synaptic weight such that weak inputs potentiate and strong inputs depress.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental manipulations and computational modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: A network model implementing bidirectional synaptic learning rule suggested that BTSP enables population activity, rather than pairwise neuronal correlations, to drive neural adaptations to experience.
source: A network model implementing this bidirectional synaptic learning rule suggested that BTSP enables population activity, rather than pairwise neuronal correlations, to drive neural adaptations to experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic plasticity plays an important role in various forms of spatial and episodic learning and memory in the hippocampus.
source: In the hippocampus, synaptic plasticity plays an important role in various forms of spatial and episodic learning and memory (Nakazawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The spatial firing rates of hippocampal place cells have been shown to be modified by experience and by changes in environmental context or the locations of salient features.
source: The spatial firing rates of hippocampal place cells have been shown to be modified by experience and by changes in environmental context or the locations of salient features (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Mehta et al., 1997; Lever et al., 2002; Dupret et al., 2010; Zaremba et al., 2017; Turi et al., 2019; Ziv et al., 2013; Muller and Kubie, 1987; Bostock et al., 1991; Fyhn et al., 2007; Leutgeb et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Place field modifications can occur rapidly, even within a single trial.
source: These modifications can occur rapidly, even within a single trial (Hill, 1978; Mehta, 2015; Monaco et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Jezek et al., 2011; Geiller et al., 2017; Bourboulou et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hebbian synaptic plasticity mechanisms are autonomously driven by repeated synchronous activity between synaptically connected neurons.
source: The core feature of such plasticity mechanisms is that they are autonomously driven by repeated synchronous activity between synaptically connected neurons, which results in either increases or decreases in synaptic strength depending on the exact temporal coincidence (Gerstner et al., 2018; Keck et al., 2017; Shouval et al., 2010; Song et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement describes established features of Hebbian plasticity, supported by citations.

claim: Three-factor plasticity rules depend on pre- and postsynaptic activity plus a third factor that extends the time course over which plasticity can function.
source: This includes the so-called 'three-factor' plasticity rules that, in addition to pre- and postsynaptic activity, depend on a third factor that extends the time course over which plasticity can function (Magee and Grienberger, 2020; Gerstner et al., 2018; He et al., 2015; Yagishita et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes three-factor plasticity rules, supported by citations.

claim: BTSP rapidly modifies synaptic inputs active within a seconds-long time window around the plateau potential.
source: This form of synaptic plasticity, termed behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), rapidly modifies synaptic inputs active within a seconds-long time window around the plateau potential.
evidence: This statement describes a key feature of BTSP based on prior research findings.

claim: BTSP was shown to strengthen many synaptic inputs whose activation did not coincide with any postsynaptic spiking or even subthreshold depolarization detected at the soma.
source: However, BTSP was shown to strengthen many synaptic inputs whose activation did not coincide with any postsynaptic spiking or even subthreshold depolarization detected at the soma (Bittner et al., 2017), suggesting that changes in synaptic weight might be independent of correlated pre- and postsynaptic activity, and that BTSP may be fundamentally different than all variants of Hebbian synaptic plasticity (Gerstner et al., 2018; Keck et al., 2017; Shouval et al., 2010; Mehta, 2004; Golding et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and includes an inference about the implications.

claim: Dendritic plateau potentials rapidly translocate the place field position of hippocampal place cells, both by strengthening inputs active near the plateau position and weakening inputs active within the original place field.
source: We found that dendritic plateau potentials rapidly translocate the place field position of hippocampal place cells, both by strengthening inputs active near the plateau position and weakening inputs active within the original place field.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The direction of plasticity induced by plateau potentials is independent of postsynaptic depolarization and spiking.
source: In order to determine if the increased postsynaptic activity in place cells is causally related to the synaptic depression observed within the initial place field, we performed a series of voltage perturbation experiments, which indicated that the direction of plasticity induced by plateau potentials is independent of postsynaptic depolarization and spiking.
evidence: This conclusion is based on voltage perturbation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The current weight of each synaptic input controls the direction of plasticity such that weak inputs potentiate and strong inputs depress.
source: Next, we inferred from the data a computational model of the synaptic learning rule underlying this bidirectional form of plasticity, which suggested that it is instead the current weight of each synaptic input that controls the direction of plasticity such that weak inputs potentiate and strong inputs depress.
evidence: This conclusion is based on computational modeling informed by experimental data.

claim: Intracellular voltage recordings were established from CA1 pyramidal neurons in head-fixed mice trained to run for a water reward on a circular treadmill.
source: Intracellular voltage recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons were established in head-fixed mice trained to run for a water reward on a circular treadmill decorated with visual and tactile cues to distinguish spatial positions (~185 cm in length).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Brief step currents (700 pA, 300 ms) were injected through the intracellular electrode to evoke plateau potentials at a second location.
source: Brief step currents (700 pA, 300 ms) were injected through the intracellular electrode for a small number (Nakazawa et al., 2004; O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Mehta et al., 1997; Lever et al., 2002; Dupret et al., 2010; Zaremba et al., 2017; Turi et al., 2019; Ziv et al., 2013) of consecutive laps to evoke plateau potentials at a second location that was between 0 and 150 cm from the initial place field (labeled 'Induction 2' in Figure 1A and B; n = 26 plasticity inductions in 24 neurons).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: In 8/24 neurons a 'natural' pre-existing place field was expressed from the start of recording, while in 16/24 the initial place field was first experimentally induced.
source: In 8/24 neurons a 'natural' pre-existing place field was expressed from the start of recording, while in 16/24 the initial place field was first experimentally induced by the same procedure (labeled 'Induction 1' in Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and sample composition.

claim: Evoked dendritic plateaus shifted the location of the neuron's pre-existing place field toward the position of the second induction site in most cases.
source: In most cases the evoked dendritic plateaus shifted the location of the neuron's pre-existing place field toward the position of the second induction site (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Place field firing is driven by a slow, ramping depolarization of Vm from sub- to supra-threshold levels.
source: Place field firing is known to be driven by a slow, ramping depolarization of Vm from sub- to supra-threshold levels (Bittner et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Plateau potentials shifted the neuron's Vm ramp toward the position of the plateau, such that the new Vm ramp peaked near the plateau position in most neurons (average distance = 19.5 ± 4.7 cm; n = 26).
source: Isolation of these low-pass filtered Vm ramps (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-H; Materials and methods) revealed that plateau potentials likewise shifted the neuron's Vm ramp toward the position of the plateau, such that the new Vm ramp peaked near the plateau position in most neurons (average distance = 19.5 ± 4.7 cm; n = 26; Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; example cells shown in Figure 1C are indicated with matching colored arrows in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by quantitative data and figures.

claim: Similar shifts in place field position were induced by spontaneous, naturally occurring plateau potentials (n = 5).
source: We also observed similar shifts in place field position to be induced by spontaneous, naturally occurring plateau potentials in a separate set of recordings (n = 5; Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-M).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The increases in Vm depolarization peaked near the position of the plateau, while the negative changes peaked near the initial place field.
source: In general, the increases in Vm depolarization peaked near the position of the plateau, while the negative changes peaked near the initial place field (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The peak change in the positive direction was greater than the peak change in the negative direction (mean positive change± SEM vs. mean negative change± SEM: 6.73 ± 0.73 mV vs. 3.89 ± 0.32 mV, n = 26 inductions; p = 0.0001, paired two-way Student's t-test).
source: Although these changes varied considerably in magnitude across cells, the peak change in the positive direction was greater than the peak change in the negative direction (mean positive change± SEM vs. mean negative change± SEM: 6.73 ± 0.73 mV vs. 3.89 ± 0.32 mV, n = 26 inductions; p = 0.0001, paired two-way Student's t-test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a strong linear relationship between the width of the resulting ΔVm and the running speed of the animal during plateau induction laps.
source: In analyzing the spatial extent of the Vm changes induced by plateaus, we observed a strong linear relationship between the width of the resulting ΔVm and the running speed of the animal during plateau induction laps (Figure 2C and D), which had a slope on the order of seconds.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The positive and negative changes to Vm induced in place cells occurred over a timescale of multiple seconds.
source: This analysis showed that the positive and negative changes to Vm induced in place cells occurred over a timescale of multiple seconds (Figure 2F), with the positive changes appearing to be asymmetric with respect to the onset time of the plateaus (ratio of potentiation duration before/after plateau onset: 2.2; black circles and crossmarks in Figure 2F mark the time points when ΔVm crosses zero).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The negative changes (hyperpolarizations indicative of synaptic depression) occurred within a time window between ±2 and ±6 s from the plateau in many neurons that expressed pre-existing place fields.
source: The negative changes (i.e. the hyperpolarizations indicative of synaptic depression) occurred within a time window between ±2 and ±6 s from the plateau in many neurons that expressed pre-existing place fields (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Hyperpolarization was greatly reduced or absent in place cells where the time delay between plateau onset and the initial place field Vm ramp was greater than 4–5 s.
source: Notably, this hyperpolarization was greatly reduced, or even absent, in a set of place cells where the time delay between plateau onset and the initial place field Vm ramp was greater than 4–5 s (red traces in Figures 1C, 2A and E; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F), further indicating the time delimited aspect of the depression component.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: BTSP is a bidirectional form of synaptic plasticity with a seconds-long timescale that enables dendritic plateau potentials to shift the locations of hippocampal place fields by inducing both synaptic potentiation and depression.
source: These data reinforce the idea that BTSP is a bidirectional form of synaptic plasticity with a seconds-long timescale that enables dendritic plateau potentials to shift the locations of hippocampal place fields by inducing both synaptic potentiation and depression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The change in Vm (ΔVm) induced by plateaus showed a more consistent shape in time that appeared to depend on the initial level of Vm depolarization at each time point prior to plasticity.
source: In contrast, the change in Vm (ΔVm) induced by plateaus showed a more consistent shape in time that appeared to depend on the initial level of Vm depolarization at each time point prior to plasticity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Large positive changes occurred at time points with relatively hyperpolarized initial Vm, while time points with more depolarized initial Vm were associated with less positive and more negative ΔVm.
source: Large positive changes occurred at time points with relatively hyperpolarized initial Vm, while time points with more depolarized initial Vm were associated with less positive and more negative ΔVm.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the data analysis.

claim: BTSP induces variable changes in synaptic strength that reshape the selectivity of neurons toward a common target shape – a place field centered near the location of evoked plateau potentials that decays toward baseline over many seconds in each direction.
source: These results indicate that BTSP induces variable changes in synaptic strength that reshape the selectivity of neurons toward a common target shape – a place field centered near the location of evoked plateau potentials that decays toward baseline over many seconds in each direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: More depression and less potentiation was induced in place cells at spatial positions that were initially most depolarized.
source: Indeed, more depression and less potentiation was induced in place cells at those spatial positions that were initially most depolarized (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: ΔVm showed a strong inverse correlation with initial Vm (m = –0.91) when all spatial bins from all place cells were analyzed.
source: Indeed, when all spatial bins from all place cells were analyzed, ΔVm showed a strong inverse correlation with initial Vm (m = –0.91; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Final Vm showed a very weak positive correlation with initial Vm (m = 0.04).
source: In contrast, final Vm showed a very weak positive correlation with initial Vm (m = 0.04; Figure 3H), which reflects that some spatial bins show no change in Vm during plasticity, either because they were traversed outside the temporal window for plasticity or because the Vm at those positions had already reached a final Vm target value.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding with an interpretation.

claim: The depression of Vm in place cells appeared to be weaker than the potentiation, leaving some residual depolarization at positions distant from the peak.
source: It should also be noted that the depression of Vm in place cells appeared to be weaker than the potentiation, leaving some residual depolarization at positions distant from the peak (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in figures.

claim: BTSP may induce synaptic depression at a slower rate than potentiation.
source: The functional significance of this is unclear, but may suggest that BTSP induces synaptic depression at a slower rate than potentiation (Cone and Shouval, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by a citation.

claim: The increased Vm depolarization within a cell's place field reflects the activation of strongly weighted synaptic inputs, which have been potentiated by prior plasticity.
source: Furthermore, the increased Vm depolarization within a cell's place field also reflects the activation of strongly weighted synaptic inputs, which have been potentiated by prior plasticity (Bittner et al., 2015; Bittner et al., 2017; Figure 3J).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and a figure in the manuscript.

claim: Somatic voltage manipulations are not expected to strictly control or completely overwhelm Vm at the synaptic sites relevant to plasticity induction due to attenuation of current and voltage along the dendritic cable.
source: It is important to note that these somatic voltage manipulations are not expected to strictly control or even completely overwhelm Vm at the synaptic sites relevant to plasticity induction (Magee and Johnston, 1997; Koester and Sakmann, 1998; Froemke et al., 2005) due to attenuation of current and voltage along the dendritic cable (Magee, 1998; Golding et al., 2005), and compartmentalization of synaptic voltage in dendritic spines (Harnett et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on dendritic cable properties.

claim: Manipulation of somatic Vm and spike timing will alter the number of action potentials that back-propagate into dendrites, which will influence the activation of voltage-gated channels in dendrites and spines.
source: However, by either increasing or decreasing the generation of somatic action potentials, this manipulation will unequivocally alter the number of action potentials that back-propagate into dendrites, which will in turn influence the activation of voltage-gated channels in dendrites and spines (e.g. Na+ channels, Ca2+ channels, and NMDA-Rs) (Magee and Johnston, 1997; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on back-propagating action potentials.

claim: Expected changes to the mean Vm in active dendritic spines were supported by simulations of a biophysically and morphologically detailed CA1 place cell model.
source: Expected changes to the mean Vm in active dendritic spines were supported by simulations of a biophysically and morphologically detailed CA1 place cell model expressing voltage-gated ion channels and receiving rhythmic excitation and inhibition to mimic the in vivo recording conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Grienberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by computational modeling results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In spatially untuned silent cells depolarized by ~10 mV during plasticity induction, plateau potentials induced large positive ΔVm at spatial positions surrounding the plateau location, and no negative ΔVm at any spatial positions.
source: According to the above scheme, we first recorded from spatially untuned silent cells, and injected current (~100 pA) through the intracellular pipette to depolarize the neurons' Vm by ~10 mV and to increase spiking during plasticity induction trials (Figure 4A; baseline trials mean AP rate: 0.26 ± 0.25 Hz; first induction trial mean AP rate: 4.8 ± 1.4 Hz, n = 8; blue trace in Figure 4B). In all neurons tested, we observed plateau potentials to induce large positive ΔVm at spatial positions surrounding the plateau location, and no negative ΔVm at any spatial positions (Figure 4A; blue trace in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: The result of depolarizing silent cells during plasticity induction is inconsistent with a causal dependence on initial Vm.
source: This result is inconsistent with a causal dependence on initial Vm (Figure 3K), which predicted a ΔVm profile similar to that of control place cells at their most depolarized positions within their pre-existing place fields (red traces, 'control PCs (within-field)' in Figure 4B and C repeated from Figure 3D and E for comparison).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of the hypothesis being tested.

claim: In place cells hyperpolarized by ~–15 mV at spatial locations surrounding their pre-existing place fields during plasticity induction at a second location, negative ΔVm was still observed at positions within the original place field.
source: Next, we performed the inverse manipulation by recording from place cells and injecting current (~–150 pA) to hyperpolarize the neurons' Vm by ~–15 mV and prevent spiking at spatial locations surrounding their pre-existing place fields while plasticity was induced at a second location (Figure 4D; baseline trials in-field mean AP rate 10.66 ± 0.93 Hz; first induction trial in-field mean AP rate 0.06 ± 0.06 Hz, n = 5; green trace in Figure 4E). This manipulation did not prevent negative ΔVm at positions within the original place field (Figure 4D; green trace in Figure 4F), again incompatible with synaptic depression requiring elevated postsynaptic depolarization and spiking (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: Full amplitude synaptic depression was observed at locations within the original place field despite the somatic Vm being more hyperpolarized than either the silent cell or control place cell groups.
source: In fact, full amplitude synaptic depression was observed at locations within the original place field despite the somatic Vm being more hyperpolarized than either the silent cell (black traces in Figure 4E and F) or control place cell groups (red traces, 'control PCs' in Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: The direction of plasticity induced by dendritic plateau potentials is not determined by the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron.
source: These data clearly show that the direction of plasticity induced by dendritic plateau potentials is not determined by the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: The initial strength of each synapse controls whether an input will be potentiated or depressed by BTSP.
source: Instead, the results of these voltage perturbation experiments support the alternative hypothesis that it is the initial strength of each synapse that controls whether an input will be potentiated or depressed by BTSP (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: The magnitude of potentiation and depression was slightly affected by the voltage perturbations.
source: However, the magnitude of potentiation and depression was slightly affected by the voltage perturbations (e.g. potentiation was slightly but significantly increased in silent cells during artificial depolarization compared to control, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: BTSP induction requires activation of voltage-dependent ion channels, including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDA-Rs) and voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: This is consistent with the previously reported finding that BTSP induction requires activation of voltage-dependent ion channels, including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDA-Rs) and voltage-gated calcium channels (Bittner et al., 2017), which would have predicted BTSP to depend on postsynaptic depolarization.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Strong hyperpolarization of silent cells (~–50 mV for ~3 s just before plateau initiation) during plasticity induction decreased synaptic potentiation.
source: To examine this further, we performed an additional set of experiments in which silent cells were strongly hyperpolarized by somatic current injection (~–50 mV for ~3 s just before plateau initiation) during plasticity induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This manipulation decreased synaptic potentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with a requirement for activation of voltage-dependent NMDA-Rs.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from additional voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: A large, non-physiological level of global Vm hyperpolarization was required to alter BTSP, reinforcing that the dependence is not on voltage signals associated with neuronal activation state, but rather on those associated with synaptic input.
source: That such a large, non-physiological level of global Vm hyperpolarization was required to alter BTSP reinforces the finding that, operationally, the dependence is not on voltage signals associated with neuronal activation state (sustained somatodendritic Vm and action potentials), but rather on those associated with synaptic input (transient local spine depolarization) (Beaulieu-Laroche and Harnett, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, supported by a citation.

claim: The voltage perturbation experiments do not support a role for synaptic depolarization in determining the direction of changes in synaptic strengths.
source: Finally, these experiments do not support a role for synaptic depolarization in determining the direction of changes in synaptic strengths.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: The form of synaptic plasticity underlying BTSP does not depend on the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron.
source: The above voltage perturbation experiments suggested that the form of synaptic plasticity underlying BTSP does not depend on the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: BTSP contrasts with Hebbian plasticity rules that typically depend on either the firing rate or depolarization of the postsynaptic cell to determine the amplitude and direction of changes in synaptic weight.
source: This contrasts with Hebbian plasticity rules that typically depend on either the firing rate or depolarization of the postsynaptic cell to determine the amplitude and direction of changes in synaptic weight.
evidence: This is a comparison between BTSP and Hebbian plasticity based on established knowledge.

claim: BTSP appears to be inherently stable, converting synaptic potentiation into depression when input strengths exceed a particular range.
source: Another difference is that BTSP appears to be inherently stable, converting synaptic potentiation into depression when input strengths exceed a particular range, whereas most models of Hebbian learning require additional homeostatic mechanisms to counteract synaptic potentiation in highly active neurons (Oja, 1982; Bienenstock et al., 1982; Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Zenke et al., 2013; Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison between BTSP and Hebbian learning models, supported by citations.

claim: BTSP induces both potentiation and depression that depend on the timing of presynaptic spiking relative to postsynaptic plateau potentials and the current weight of each synapse.
source: In this 'weight-dependent' model, the direction and magnitude of plasticity at excitatory synapses from spatially tuned CA3 place cell inputs onto a CA1 pyramidal cell are determined by (1) the timing of presynaptic spiking relative to postsynaptic plateau potentials and (2) the current weight of each synapse just prior to a plateau.
evidence: This describes the key features of the computational model developed in the study.

claim: The weight-dependent model of BTSP contained nine free parameters, which were fit to the experimental data using an iterative, bounded, stochastic search procedure based on the simulated annealing algorithm.
source: This model contained nine free parameters (described in detail below), which were fit to the experimental data using an iterative, bounded, stochastic search procedure based on the simulated annealing algorithm (Milstein, 2021a; Milstein, 2021b).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling methods used in the study.

claim: The weight-dependent model quantitatively matched the experimental data across all cells.
source: Across all cells, these predictions quantitatively matched the corresponding experimental data (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result of the computational modeling, supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The sensitivity of changes in Vm to initial Vm and time to plateau predicted by the model recapitulated that measured from the in vivo intracellular recordings.
source: Finally, the sensitivity of changes in Vm to initial Vm and time to plateau predicted by the model recapitulated that measured from the in vivo intracellular recordings (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result of the computational modeling, supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Intermediate signals with durations longer than either voltage or calcium are required for the long timescale of BTSP.
source: This supports the notion that intermediate signals with durations longer than either voltage or calcium are required for the long timescale of BTSP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The network model implementing bidirectional BTSP recapitulated experimentally observed modifications in CA1 network activity during goal-directed behavior.
source: Overall, this resulted in an increased proportion of place cells with fields near the goal position (Figure 7E, right), recapitulating experimentally observed modifications in CA1 network activity during goal-directed behavior (Zaremba et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result of the network modeling, supported by comparison to prior experimental findings.

claim: The asymmetric time course of BTSP caused the population representation of the goal in the model to peak before the goal location itself, producing a predictive memory representation of the path leading to the goal.
source: The asymmetric time course of BTSP caused the population representation of the goal in the model to peak before the goal location itself, producing a predictive memory representation of the path leading to the goal (Mehta et al., 1997; Stachenfeld et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result of the network modeling, supported by citations to related work.

claim: Plasticity regulated by local network activity and long-range feedback, rather than by pairwise correlations, can enable populations of place cells to rapidly adapt their spatial representations to changes in the environment without any compromise in selectivity.
source: These network modeling results demonstrate that plasticity regulated by local network activity and long-range feedback, rather than by pairwise correlations, can enable populations of place cells to rapidly adapt their spatial representations to changes in the environment without any compromise in selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the network modeling results.

claim: Changes in place field firing in CA1 could be induced by juxtacellular current injection, which was correlated with the occurrence of long duration complex spikes.
source: These results corroborate recent work showing that changes in place field firing in CA1 could be induced by juxtacellular current injection, which was correlated with the occurrence of long duration complex spikes (Diamantaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The time and synaptic weight dependence of BTSP suggests that it is driven by an input-specific process rather than nonselective heterosynaptic or homeostatic plasticity, or modulation of cellular excitability.
source: The time and synaptic weight dependence of BTSP suggests that it is driven by an input-specific process rather than nonselective heterosynaptic (Lynch et al., 1977) or homeostatic plasticity (Mendez et al., 2018; Hengen et al., 2016), or modulation of cellular excitability (Chandra and Barkai, 2018; Titley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: A significant role for changes in inhibitory synaptic weights is unlikely given that inhibitory neurons in CA1 exhibit low levels of spatial selectivity, homosynaptic potentiation of excitatory inputs by dendritic plateau potentials can be induced with GABAergic inhibition blocked, and inhibitory input to CA1 neurons does not change following induction of synaptic potentiation by BTSP.
source: A significant role for changes in inhibitory synaptic weights is unlikely given that (1) inhibitory neurons in CA1 exhibit low levels of spatial selectivity (Grienberger et al., 2017), (2) homosynaptic potentiation of excitatory inputs by dendritic plateau potentials can be induced with GABAergic inhibition blocked (Bittner et al., 2017), and (3) inhibitory input to CA1 neurons does not change following induction of synaptic potentiation by BTSP (Grienberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BTSP does not depend on the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron, pointing to a fundamental difference between BTSP and existing Hebbian models of plasticity.
source: The voltage perturbation experiments we performed (Figure 4) showed that BTSP does not depend on the activation state of the postsynaptic neuron. These results point to a fundamental difference between BTSP and existing Hebbian models of plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage perturbation experiments.

claim: In most previous models of plasticity, the firing rate or sustained level of global depolarization at the time of presynaptic spiking primarily determines whether a synaptic weight increases or decreases.
source: In most previous models, including the aforementioned 'three-factor' plasticity models, the firing rate (He et al., 2015; Brzosko et al., 2015; Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998), or sustained level of global depolarization (Clopath et al., 2010; Artola et al., 1990; Brandalise and Gerber, 2014) at the time of presynaptic spiking primarily determines whether a synaptic weight increases or decreases (Gerstner et al., 2018; Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Caporale and Dan, 2008).
evidence: This statement describes features of existing plasticity models, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of dependence on postsynaptic activity could enable plasticity to be robust to fluctuations in postsynaptic state due to noise or network oscillations.
source: This lack of dependence on the postsynaptic activity or output could enable plasticity to be robust to fluctuations in postsynaptic state due to noise or network oscillations (e.g. theta or gamma) (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013), and may allow the postsynaptic state to subserve other functions, such as temporal coding, without interfering with ongoing synaptic weight modifications.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: BTSP provides a mechanism to either create new pairwise activity correlations 'from scratch', or remove pre-existing ones based on delayed outcomes.
source: Furthermore, while in traditional Hebbian models of plasticity, short timescale synchrony between pre- and postsynaptic activity modifies weights to reinforce pre-existing correlations, BTSP instead provides a mechanism to either create new pairwise activity correlations 'from scratch', or remove pre-existing ones based on delayed outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional implications of BTSP compared to Hebbian plasticity.

claim: If plateau potentials are generated by a mismatch between local circuit output and target information relayed by long-range feedback, BTSP can implement objective-based learning.
source: This model also demonstrated that, if plateau potentials are generated by a mismatch between local circuit output and target information relayed by long-range feedback, BTSP can implement objective-based learning (Richards et al., 2019b; Sacramento, 2018; Payeur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network modeling, supported by citations to related work.
